nameStory: This tiny green algae gets its scientific name from Otto Kirchner, a 19th-century German botanist who studied freshwater algae. The species name 'obesa' means 'fat' or 'plump' in Latin, referring to the chubby, rounded shape of its individual cells that look like tiny green balloons under a microscope.
description: Kirchneriella obesa is a microscopic freshwater algae that forms loose colonies of crescent-shaped to oval cells floating in ponds, lakes, and slow streams. Each individual cell is so tiny you'd need a microscope to see it clearly, but colonies can sometimes create a faint greenish tinge in the water. The cells are notably plump and rounded compared to other algae, giving them their 'obesa' name. This single-celled organism is part of the green algae family and plays an important role in aquatic ecosystems.

idTips.label: Cell Shape
idTips.description: Individual cells are distinctly plump and oval to crescent-shaped, noticeably fatter than most other green algae when viewed under magnification

idTips.label: Colony Formation
idTips.description: Forms loose, irregular clusters of cells that drift freely in the water rather than forming tight, structured colonies

idTips.label: Water Appearance
idTips.description: May create a subtle greenish tint in calm water bodies, though individual organisms are invisible to the naked eye

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Found in still or slow-moving freshwater with adequate nutrients, often in areas with some organic matter

habitat: Kirchneriella obesa lives in freshwater environments throughout New England, particularly in nutrient-rich ponds, quiet lake coves, and slow-moving streams. It thrives in areas with some organic matter and adequate sunlight for photosynthesis. You're most likely to encounter it in lowland water bodies rather than high-elevation mountain lakes.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as water temperatures rise and sunlight increases, though they remain microscopic and generally unnoticeable.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when colonies are most abundant in warm, nutrient-rich waters with plenty of sunlight for photosynthesis.
seasonality.fall: Populations may persist but typically decline as temperatures drop and daylight hours decrease.
seasonality.winter: Generally dormant or present in very low numbers, surviving as resting cells until spring conditions return.

funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, a single drop of pond water can contain thousands of these tiny organisms, and they're so efficient at photosynthesis that they produce a significant portion of the oxygen in freshwater ecosystems - you could be breathing oxygen made by these microscopic 'fat' cells!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close relative Kirchneriella lunaris, which has more distinctly crescent-shaped (moon-like) cells. Remember: obesa cells are plumper and rounder, while lunaris cells are more curved like a crescent moon - think 'obese and round' versus 'lunar and curved.'
contextualKnowledge: Like many microscopic algae, Kirchneriella species are often overlooked despite their ecological importance. They're indicators of water quality and nutrient levels, and their presence or absence can tell scientists about the health of freshwater ecosystems.
compareHints: Compared to its relative Kirchneriella lunaris, obesa has notably plumper, more oval-shaped cells rather than the distinctly crescent or moon-shaped cells of lunaris. While both form loose colonies in freshwater, obesa cells appear more rounded and 'inflated' under microscopic examination. Both species prefer similar freshwater habitats but can be distinguished reliably by their cell morphology.
